entries.title: Pinot Noir: Inside the Criminal Gangs Making Fake Wine
entries.summary: "Fraudsters have long counterfeited high-end wine. Now they are coming for the bottles on your supermarket shelves."
entries.content:
While wine fraud has been around for nearly 150 years, it exploded around the turn of the century, with enterprising counterfeiters drawn by high margins and relatively low risk. Now, though, with the highest-end manufacturers upping their game, would-be forgers are looking at more moderately priced targets; they’ve even come for mass-market brands like Yellow Tail. For 1843, William Ralston uncorks the zero-somm game.

Other popular anti-counterfeiting techniques used by high-end wineries include manufacturing proprietary bottle shapes and micro-printing, where text and patterns are printed at a scale visible only under magnification. (I was shown a bottle of 2009 Le Pin, a fine Bordeaux wine, where the names of the winery owner’s children had been micro-printed repeatedly between two thin red lines on its front label.) Some wineries have adopted advanced security measures, incorporating features like holograms, individualised digital tracking codes and inks that change colour when tilted. Pétrus, a Bordeaux winery which produces only 30,000 bottles a year, uses inks custom-made by the same company that produces the ones used on American dollar bills.

entries.title: Inside the Trial of Russell Brand
entries.summary: "Tom Lee sat through all 18 days of the would-be guru’s trial."
entries.content:
Tom Lee provides an excellent account of Russell Brand’s trial. Alongside the details—including Brand’s bizarre entourage and the defence’s unusual approach to the disturbing allegations—he describes his personal experience of the courtroom atmosphere. Lee follows the trial through to its conclusion: Brand was convicted of rape against one complainant and three other sexual assaults, and acquitted of two other rape charges.

In particular, she returned to the humiliation of being told to clear up after the rape – and her shame that she did so. Although, over the years, as she suffered from anxiety and later developed an alcohol problem, she told people she trusted what had happened to her, she could not bring herself to go to the police. She blamed herself, because she had gone to Brand’s house willingly, and did not want to become known and defined by what he had done to her.

When the last of these witness statements had been read, and the judge sent the jury out for the day, the argument that this accuser only decided she had been raped once the wider allegations had emerged seemed fatally undermined. The journalist next to me murmured: “He’s cooked.”

entries.title: When Anesthesia Goes Wrong
entries.summary: "A teenage boy went into surgery for a broken arm and emerged with brain damage. His mother was determined to figure out what had happened."
entries.content:
A teenage boy went into surgery for a broken arm and emerged with brain damage. His mother was determined to figure out what had happened. Turns out, he wasn’t the only young person adversely affected by anesthesia. A riveting medical mystery from Sarah Zhang:

Over the years, Yaremy had talked with colleagues in Venezuela about Uli so relentlessly that word sometimes came back to her of similar cases: nearly always kids, nearly always after routine surgery. An introvert by nature, Yaremy had to learn to badger anyone and everyone for a useful crumb of information.

She began running down some of these rumors: The wife of the son of a friend knew a neurologist who knew an anesthesiologist who knew of a boy who had fallen ill after surgery on a broken forearm. He became patient four. Patient five was the boy whose mother she’d met picking up Botox in Caracas. A physical therapist told her about a boy who’d had cleft-lip surgery—patient six. An old friend from medical school, an anesthesiologist, had examined a boy who developed symptoms after surgery for a cochlear implant. The friend had once been skeptical of Yaremy’s theory, but now he helped her gather data. This boy became the seventh and final patient in the study. . . . A haunting pattern appeared in the cases she was able to pull together. All seven patients in the study had received sevoflurane. Most of them could trace their maternal relatives to Carabobo; Yaremy’s own maternal grandmother was from the state. And all seven had the same T-to-C mutation.

entries.title: Bright Star
entries.summary: "A mixed-age permaculture school in Mexico is showing how an education based on autonomy and care prepares students better for life."
entries.content:
In this essay, part of Earth Island Journal’s autumn 2026 issue, Sarah Menkedick highlights a Montessori-inspired school in Ensenada, Mexico, that fosters in its children autonomy, real-world responsibility, and a deep connection to nature. Menkedick, an instructor at the University of Pittsburgh, sees a disconnect between her own college-age students and their natural environments, and reflects on the outdated, one-size-fits-all education system in the US.

In talking about school, we often use the term “material.” What material will the students study? This tends to refer to the curricula, and those curricula are largely formed of abstract knowledge contained in worksheets, textbooks, or software, which students practice and master. But the material of Cocuy is tangible: It is mud, brick, paint, glass. It is herb, sun, animal, mineral. It is popo. And, also, it is the individual, embodied human being, a complex part of the whole. Cocuy calls itself a “permaculture school,” but it does not ask students to simply study nature but rather to inhabit and know it.

“As wildlife advocates fight to free the last captives of Vietnam’s bile farms, rescued bears find dignity in the country’s sanctuaries.”

“In America, whether we can swim — and whether we have access to water at all — is closely tied to race.”

entries.title: The Downfall of a Top Cop
entries.summary: Willy Van Mechelen was one of the most celebrated police officers in Belgian history, responsible for solving infamous kidnappings, robberies, and murders. Then Antwerp’s lucrative drug trade came calling.
entries.content:
Alessio Perrone and Berber Verpoest | The Atavist Magazine | October 2026 | 2,080 words (7 minutes)

This is an excerpt from issue no. 181, “The Rise and Fall of a Super-Cop.”

The shipping container came from Costa Rica, and it was supposed to hold timber. When it arrived in the Belgian city of Antwerp in October 2019, the steel box with tracking number TCKU1048144 was loaded into what looked like a massive game of Tetris: As Europe’s second-largest port, handling some 290 million metric tons of cargo every year, Antwerp holds tens of thousands of shipping containers at any moment, painted in bright hues and arranged in long, neat rows. From the outside, nothing seemed amiss with TCKU1048144, which is exactly what the drug traffickers who’d packed it intended.

Cocaine had been flooding into Antwerp for at least a decade. After Mexican cartels took over the U.S. market, Colombian traffickers looked to Europe, and Antwerp’s port provided them with readymade infrastructure to shuttle their product onto the continent. The cocaine trade warped life in the city. As gangs fought for control, Antwerp was rocked by car bombings, shootings, and other violence. Local media reported on houses battered by grenades as the worst of the city’s underworld attempted to intimidate rivals and snitches. Corruption spread, with trafficking networks paying off port workers, cops, hospital staff—anyone they needed to look the other way.

The Atavist, our sister publication, publishes one deeply reported, elegantly designed story each month. Support The Atavist by becoming a member.

Customs agents found themselves on the front lines of an escalating war, trying to keep cocaine out of Belgium against what seemed like impossible odds. Antwerp’s government had boosted funding for personnel, technology, and other investigative resources, helping customs increase the amount of cocaine it seized each year; the figure more than doubled between 2016 and 2019. Still, European demand for coke was stratospheric, and suppliers were determined to meet it. Powder just kept coming.

On October 28, container TCKU1048144 was selected for X-ray inspection. Containers moving through Antwerp’s port can be designated for a scan at random or for any number of logistical reasons, including improper documentation or suspicious shipping information. The X-ray showed that there was timber inside TCKU1048144, as its paperwork indicated, but agents spotted something else beneath the wood—bags, from the look of it. They opened the container’s heavy doors and found taped-up slabs of cocaine, 2,792 kilograms’ worth. There was also a counterfeit container seal, left by the South American traffickers for the shipment’s European recipients. By resealing the box after removing the drugs, the criminals could make it look as though no one had tampered with TCKU1048144.

Law enforcement decided to let the container continue on to the destination indicated on its paperwork: Maasmechelen, a sleepy town sixty miles southeast of Antwerp. They hoped that this tactic would help them identify and eventually arrest key players in the trafficking network. Customs removed the cocaine, resealed the container, then kept watch over it. The next evening, a driver arrived to pick it up. Law enforcement followed him, but instead of heading toward Maasmechelen, he went north, speeding to the Dutch border. He crossed over and stopped at a warehouse in Zevenbergen, a small city on the Rhine estuary. Outside were several vehicles, including an Audi SUV.

As police watched from a distance, they got a look at the man in the Audi. He was elderly, with steely blue eyes and dark hair. It didn’t take long to identify him. In fact, plenty of people in Belgian law enforcement knew him by sight. His name was Willy Van Mechelen, and once upon a time, he’d been the most famous cop in the country.

Chapter 1

Willy Karel Ferdinand Van Mechelen was born in 1943 into a Catholic family in a middle-class suburb of Antwerp. He spent much of his childhood at his grandfather’s mill in a hamlet in the Kempen, an area between Antwerp and the Dutch border known for its farms and wetlands. Van Mechelen was an exuberant, rebellious boy. When his peers dared him to climb onto a windmill’s rotating blades, he would race to do it. If a priest told him to be quiet during mass, he would storm out of church. According to a memoir he published in 1997, he and his two brothers never caused any serious trouble, but they got up to so much mischief that they became known to their neighbors as “the Dalton brothers,” after a fabled gang of outlaws in the American frontier. (In addition to that memoir, this article is based on dozens of hours of interviews with sources, hundreds of pages of court documents, and several books written by Van Mechelen’s contemporaries.)

During his senior year of high school, Van Mechelen decided to drop out. His father, who worked as a gendarme, had acquaintances at a shipping agency in Antwerp and secured his son a position clearing goods through customs. The job wasn’t exactly adrenaline pumping, even if obtaining stamps from Belgian customs sometimes required greasing the right palms. But Van Mechelen was able to spend his days outdoors, roaming among the terminals of the city’s huge port.

When he turned 18, he began his mandatory military service, and the army gave him direction and purpose. He became a paratrooper and deployed to Burundi, which at that point was still part of a Belgian colony. After fifteen months, he returned to the shipping company a changed man. He was more confident but also more impatient, easily frustrated by older colleagues he would later dismiss as “mummies” who only talked about retirement.

One day a customs agent asked him for a larger than usual bribe. Van Mechelen was unfazed and handed over the banknotes. Back in the office, his boss didn’t thank or reimburse him. Instead he lectured Van Mechelen on how to do his job properly—and did so in French instead of Dutch, the language everyone spoke in Antwerp. Van Mechelen thought that his boss was talking down to him, and he was furious. He grabbed a lectern and hurled it across the room. When he went home, he expressed an interest in his father’s line of work for the first time. Might the national police have a position for him? “That’s how I became a gendarme,” Van Mechelen wrote in his memoir, “out of rage.”

He joined the force in the late 1960s and was assigned to the mounted division, a position he detested for not seeing enough action. Eventually, he became a shooting instructor for the anti-terror squad and then joined a special unit in charge of Antwerp’s most challenging criminal investigations. The unit was known as the BOB, short for Bewakings- en Opsporingsbrigade, or Surveillance and Investigation Brigade.

Belgian law enforcement at the time operated with so few checks and balances that it more or less did as it pleased. In robbery cases where insurance companies offered rewards to informants if their tips contributed to the recovery of loot, cops sometimes roped in civilians after locating stolen items, allowing so-called informants to claim the money and then split it with the officers. The scheme was lucrative but illegal. “There was a bit of a cowboy mentality,” said Jean-Charles Verwaest, a retired journalist.

Complicating matters was the fact that Belgium had three distinct police services: the gendarmerie, a national force under the authority of the country’s interior and defense ministries; the judicial police, which reported to public prosecutors’ offices; and the municipal police, the equivalent of local law enforcement in the U.S. The gendarmerie and the judicial police in particular were locked in a power struggle. They often refused to share intelligence or even acknowledge each other’s authority. Investigations were duplicated or sabotaged, and suspects slipped through cracks widened by ego and pride. The turf struggle reached a peak in the 1980s, becoming known as the guerre des flics, or “cop war.”

Van Mechelen learned the rules of battle early. On his first case with the BOB, he let a more senior colleague drive to the crime scene, only to discover that the judicial police had arrived first and staked their claim to the investigation. “That was my first lesson at the BOB,” he later wrote. “Always get behind the wheel yourself.”

Van Mechelen quickly made a name for himself. He was the kind of man who could have a pint with anyone, and often picked up the tab when he did. Tall and broad shouldered, he cut such an imposing figure that people sometimes compared him to the Belgian comic-book character Jerom, who has superhuman strength. He became known for shows of force and for refusing to take guff from anyone. Once, during a raid, he flung a man through a ground-floor window for the offense of mocking him. “Everyone knew where the line was then,” he later wrote.

Van Mechelen could also be clever. “He was the best detective in the BOB, there’s no getting away from that,” said Walter De Smedt, a former investigative judge who led inquiries into organized crime in Antwerp and often chose to work with Van Mechelen. In those days police officers didn’t specialize. They had to do it all: investigative work, raids, interrogations. “Only Van Mechelen was very good at all of them,” De Smedt said. “If you assigned a case to him, you always got something back.”

Van Mechelen developed his own way of handling the various crimes that afflicted Antwerp, from prostitution rackets to contraband smuggling to violent robberies. When he raided a bar or restaurant during a BOB operation, he scribbled down the name of every person there, noting who was sitting with whom. Over time he developed extensive knowledge of Antwerp’s underworld. “If a robbery happened and we caught one of the perpetrators, all we had to do was check in the file catalog with whom he had been sitting in the bar the days before,” he wrote in his memoir. “Nine times out of ten, we caught the whole gang.”

Van Mechelen rose through the ranks of the BOB until he was head of an entire division. His men loved him; working for him meant plenty of action and also freedom. “There was basically no discipline,” said Guy Verhemeldonck, a former officer who later became the godfather to two of Van Mechelen’s children. (Van Mechelen had two children in the 1980s with his then-partner, and one in the 1990s after marrying another woman.) Sometimes the men had to work long hours, even pull night shifts. Other times they would leave the office in the middle of the day to grab a drink. When they did, Van Mechelen only reminded them to keep their eyes and ears open—after all, criminals hung out in bars, too.

For proof they needed to look no further than the kidnapping of Baron Charles-Victor Bracht, a diplomat, businessman, and multimillionaire. On March 7, 1978, a masked, armed man grabbed Bracht in an Antwerp garage where he’d just parked his Jaguar. The suspect, who called himself “Dexter” when communicating with authorities, asked for more than $2 million in ransom and refused to give proof of life. About a month after the abduction, he called a local newspaper and said that Bracht was dead. One week later, the baron’s body was found in a garbage dump, badly decomposed. Officers aired the perpetrator’s voice to the public, and someone recognized it as belonging to Marcel Van Tongelen, an electrician with a criminal record. But when officers showed up at his parents’ house—Van Tongelen’s registered address—they said they hadn’t seen him in years.

Van Mechelen and his men hit the bars. Armed with a name and a photograph, they went from one establishment to another around Antwerp, looking for anyone who knew the man behind the voice. An officer eventually found a mail carrier who looked at the suspect’s photo and recognized someone he occasionally had a beer with, although he knew him by a different name. The mail carrier pointed officers toward the broad avenue where the man lived. They knocked on the door of every flat until they found the suspect, four months after Bracht’s abduction.

Van Mechelen made liberal use of informants, a practice that was common among Belgian police and largely unregulated at the time. When he caught a criminal, he sometimes offered to help them avoid a harsh sentence if they provided information. “I loved working with Van Mechelen,” a one-time informant told us. “He always offered protection.”

A former member of the judicial police once said that Van Mechelen’s informants “almost seemed like [his] colleagues.” But no one considered it a problem. After all, it was hard to argue with Van Mechelen’s results.

entries.title: Maintenance Futures
entries.summary: "Future visions tend to organize around narratives of gain or loss, dystopia or utopia. But what of the neutral position?"
entries.content:
On his website, designer Christopher Butler envisions the future. As a culture, we typically default to two versions: one of less, or dystopia; and one of more, or utopia. What a limited way of thinking, no? The opposites can be the case. “A future of less can be a utopia. Not comfortably, but the case is available. The American dream is not a life that ten billion people can hold at once; the square footage, the car, the wealth per household, the arithmetic has never worked,” he writes. And then he goes on: “A future of more can also be a dystopia. I would argue that this is the corner we presently live in.” His contemplative essay explores limits, growth, creativity, and what he refers to as maintenance futurism.

Which means the idea rests on a distinction that’s easy to state and hard to keep: maintenance chosen is a practice, and maintenance imposed is a lid. Our basement storehouse is a decision we made about our present and future. It would be a different space entirely if someone had measured it out for us.

entries.title: When Idaho Banned Abortion, OB-GYNs Fled. The Doctors Who Stayed Are Cracking.
entries.summary: "From childbirth to miscarriages, women’s health care in the state has become increasingly dangerous."
entries.content:
Last week, voters in Idaho rejected a measure that would have restored the right to terminate a pregnancy up to the point of fetal viability. (The state’s abortion ban went into effect after Roe v. Wade was overturned.) It’s a devastating blow for Idaho’s women and obstetricians—those who are still practicing, that is. More than one-third of the state’s OBGYNs are no longer doing obstetrics; many have moved or retired. Today, half of Idaho’s counties do not have a practicing obstetrician. Lisa Lerer spends time with some of the state’s remaining reproductive health doctors, who are just trying to keep their heads above water:

Parker reached into her patient’s abdomen and gently jiggled and wiggled with her hands, trying to separate the spongy red disc from the uterine wall, as she had done many times before in her practice as a family-medicine doctor with a specialization in high-risk obstetrics. The organ didn’t budge. Within minutes, Parker knew what she was facing: a placenta accreta, a dangerous complication in which the placenta grows into the uterine wall.

With her hands still in her patient’s open abdomen, Parker asked her nurse to call the obstetricians. The nurse held the phone to Parker’s ear as she received the news: The OB working that morning was in Washington and would be delayed. Her patient would have to wait, lying on the surgical table with her body cut open.

entries.title: The Art of Letting Go
entries.content:
For The American Scholar, Lisa Russ Spaar offers us beautiful litany of loss in all its various shapes and forms. From those we love to objects like keys, from our teeth to our moral compass, Spaar takes a close look at what we go through when we experience loss at various times in our lives, and how losses tend to stack up as we age.

I’ve informally polled several friends, colleagues, and family members about their first remembered losses. For most, it was when a milk tooth fell out, usually around the age of six. (Surely there are primal reasons many of us dream throughout our lifetimes about our teeth, as important as they are to speaking, eating.) More than 20 years ago, one of my talented undergraduates, Molly, wrote a poem about losing her first tooth while sledding in winter. Upon tonguing the little bloody socket that remained, she wrote, “I taste my death.” That line has haunted me over the decades. Again, our bodies: made for loss. Language: our ability to articulate what that might mean.

I often wonder what was happening in my late mother’s mind as she sank, over a period of 10-plus years, into the tangled ambages of dementia. She lost the names of things and people. She lost any memory of who we were, those of us who cared for her, even her devoted husband, my father. She finally even forgot that she was not only an alcoholic with a fifth of Scotch hidden in the breadbox but also a chain smoker, though she’d occasionally hold a drinking straw to her lips and take a long, deep drag.

entries.title: The Pollycrisis
entries.content:
London’s feral parakeets are an invasive species—but they are also beautiful, and David Wingrave takes the chance to linger on their nightly roost at Hither Green Cemetery before asking whether they should be here at all. As calls for culls grow—backed by fears of crop damage, disease, and pressure on native wildlife—he probes what we really know about the harm these birds cause. Along the way, he asks deeper questions: how we decide where an animal “belongs,” when (if ever) it becomes native, and why we are so uneasy about seeing bright green birds in London’s parks.

The fix O’Gorman endorses may sound drastic, but his precautionary principle is shared by invasion biology, the subdiscipline devoted to the study of species transplanted from their native ranges. There is a long history of organisms moved by humans, whether deliberately or inadvertently, wreaking total havoc upon their new homes. The brown tree snake, native to Indonesia, northern Australia, and Papua New Guinea, was accidentally introduced to Guam by the US military following World War II and promptly ate its way through ten of the island’s twelve endemic forest bird species. Similarly, Nile perch released into Lake Victoria by British colonial forces gulped down roughly two hundred species of homegrown cichlids, fish found nowhere else on Earth. Cane toads in Australia, Miconia trees on Hawaii and Tahiti, rats just about everywhere—the list goes on. And if biodiversity loss, however regrettable, seems like an abstraction in the scheme of things, know that human culture frequently suffers direct impoverishments because of invasives. Chestnut blight, discovered in the United States in 1904 after chestnut trees were imported from Japan, effectively deleted the American chestnut tree from the continent; its products were central to the diet and lifestyles of various indigenous peoples and communities across Appalachia. Phylloxera, an aphid relative, was imported to Europe on American grapevines during the second half of the nineteenth century. The subsequent infestation resulted in the destruction, by some estimates, of 90 percent of all European vineyards.
